notes.front: For GitHub Copilot, what is the audit log?
notes.back: A record of actions in your enterprise, including Copilot plan changes (settings, policies, licences) and agent activity on GitHub.
notes.explanation: It is where administrators check who changed a Copilot setting or licence, and what agents did on the website.
notes.example: Like a building’s signing-in book, but it records who changed a Copilot policy and when.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot”
notes.evidence: You can use the audit log to review actions taken in your enterprise. The audit log includes a record of: Changes to your Copilot plan, such as changes to settings and policies or a user losing or receiving a license Agent activity on the GitHub website

notes.front: For Copilot user management, what is the REST API?
notes.back: GitHub’s set of web endpoints that manage an organization’s Copilot Business subscription from code.
notes.explanation: The Copilot user management endpoints are in public preview and subject to change.
notes.example: Like the Copilot “Access” settings page, but driven by a script instead of clicks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “REST API endpoints for Copilot user management”
notes.evidence: Use the REST API to manage the GitHub Copilot Business subscription for your organization. > [!NOTE] These endpoints are in public preview and subject to change.

notes.front: In Copilot seat management, what does “pending cancellation” mean?
notes.back: A removed seat that keeps access until the end of the current billing cycle, then loses it.
notes.explanation: The removal endpoints set seats to this state; a user who still has access through a team keeps it.
notes.example: Like a gym membership you have cancelled that still opens the door until the month runs out.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “Remove users from the Copilot subscription for an organization”
notes.evidence: Sets seats for all users specified to "pending cancellation". This will cause the specified users to lose access to GitHub Copilot at the end of the current billing cycle unless they retain access through team membership.

notes.front: In an organization’s settings, where do you edit the policies that control Copilot features?
notes.back: Under “Code, planning, and automation”, click Copilot, then Policies.
notes.explanation: Each policy has a dropdown in which you pick an enforcement option.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization, “Enabling Copilot features and models in your organization”
notes.evidence: In the sidebar, under "Code, planning, and automation", click

notes.front: An organization owner wants to turn off a Copilot feature for the members her organization licenses. Where does she go?
notes.back: A: organization Settings, then Copilot, then Policies.
notes.choices:
A) The organization’s Settings, then Copilot, then Policies
B) The repository’s Settings, then Rules
C) Her personal Copilot settings
D) The audit log
notes.choicesExplained: C covers only her own account, not the members her organization licenses. B holds repository rules, not Copilot feature policies. D records changes; it does not make them.
notes.explanation: The Policies page controls the privacy and availability of features for users the organization licenses.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization, “Enabling Copilot features and models in your organization”
notes.evidence: Click **Policies** to edit the policies that control privacy and availability of features.

notes.front: In an organization’s Copilot settings, the Policies page versus the Models page: what does each control?
notes.back: Policies: privacy and availability of features. Models: availability of models beyond the basic ones, which may cost more.
notes.explanation: Models get their own page because models beyond the basic set may incur additional costs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization, “Enabling Copilot features and models in your organization”
notes.evidence: Click **Models** to edit the policies that control availability of models beyond the basic models provided with Copilot, which may incur additional costs.

notes.front: If an enterprise owner has set a specific Copilot policy, an organization owner {{c1::cannot override}} it at the organization level.
notes.explanation: Enterprise choices such as “enabled everywhere” or “disabled everywhere” bind every organization below.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization, “Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization”
notes.evidence: If your enterprise owner has selected a specific policy, such as enabling a feature everywhere, disabling it everywhere, or enabling it for selected organizations only, you cannot override that setting at the organization level.

notes.front: For most Copilot policies, what can enterprise administrators do?
notes.back: Explicitly enable it, explicitly disable it, or let organizations decide.
notes.explanation: Policies are set at the enterprise level first; organizations choose only where the enterprise lets them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “How do policies work?”
notes.evidence: In an enterprise, policies are set at the enterprise level first. For most policies, enterprise administrators can either explicitly enable or disable a policy, or let organizations decide.

notes.front: For which Copilot feature can an enterprise pick exactly which organizations get access?
notes.back: Copilot cloud agent.
notes.explanation: It is the named exception to the usual enable, disable or “let organizations decide” choice.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “How do policies work?”
notes.evidence: As an exception, for Copilot cloud agent, enterprises can select exactly which organizations receive access.

notes.front: The enterprise has disabled Copilot CLI everywhere. An organization owner wants it on for her developers. What can she do?
notes.back: C: the enterprise setting cannot be overridden at organization level.
notes.choices:
A) Enable it in her organization’s Policies page
B) Enable it for selected members only
C) Nothing at organization level: the enterprise setting cannot be overridden
D) Ask each developer to enable it in personal settings
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: an organization cannot override a specific enterprise policy. D: licensed users are governed by the policies of whoever licenses them, not their personal settings.
notes.explanation: Only if the enterprise chose “let organizations decide” would the choice be hers.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization, “Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization”
notes.evidence: you cannot override that setting at the organization level.

notes.front: Whose policies govern a user’s Copilot?
notes.back: Those of the enterprise or organization where the user receives a Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise licence.
notes.explanation: Generally, policies apply only to users on your own Copilot plan.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “Who do policies apply to?”
notes.evidence: Generally, policies only apply to users on your Copilot plan. A user is governed by the policies of the enterprise or organization where they receive a Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise license.

notes.front: Do any Copilot policies govern a setting for everyone, not just your licensed users?
notes.back: Yes, a small number, such as blocking Copilot cloud agent for all users in your enterprise’s repositories.
notes.explanation: The policy description highlights when a policy works this way.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “Who do policies apply to?”
notes.evidence: A small number of policies work differently and govern a setting for everyone. For example, you can block Copilot cloud agent for all users in your enterprise's repositories.

notes.front: What happens to a user’s individual Copilot plan when they are added to a Copilot Business or Enterprise plan?
notes.back: It is cancelled, so their personal policies cannot conflict with the organization’s or enterprise’s.
notes.explanation: This leaves only organization and enterprise policies to reconcile.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “What about users with multiple licenses?”
notes.evidence: A user's individual plan is cancelled when they are added to a Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise plan, so a user's personal policies cannot conflict with an enterprise's or organization's.

notes.front: An outside contributor with her own Copilot Pro plan opens a pull request in your organization’s repository. Your organization has disabled a Copilot feature. Does your policy govern her Copilot?
notes.back: C: generally, policies apply only to users on your plan.
notes.choices:
A) Yes: the repository’s owner sets the policy
B) Yes: all users in the organization are covered
C) No: generally, policies apply only to users on your Copilot plan
D) Only if she accepts the organization’s terms
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: a user is governed where they receive a Business or Enterprise licence, and she does not receive one from you. D: no such acceptance step is described.
notes.explanation: Only a few policies, flagged in their descriptions, govern a setting for everyone.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “Who do policies apply to?”
notes.evidence: Generally, policies only apply to users on your Copilot plan.

notes.front: When organizations in the same enterprise set one policy differently for a user, the {{c1::least restrictive}} policy usually applies.
notes.explanation: “Usually”: GitHub notes there are some exceptions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “What about users with multiple licenses?”
notes.evidence: If these organizations have configured the same policy differently, the least restrictive policy usually applies, but there are some exceptions.

notes.front: Dev gets Copilot from two organizations in one enterprise. One enables a feature, the other disables it. What usually happens?
notes.back: C: enabled, as the least restrictive policy usually applies.
notes.choices:
A) The organization that licensed him first decides
B) The feature is disabled: the most restrictive always applies
C) The feature is enabled: the least restrictive policy usually applies
D) He chooses in his personal settings
notes.choicesExplained: B describes licences from different enterprises, and even there it is “almost always”. A: nothing ties the outcome to which came first. D: licensed users are governed by organization and enterprise policies.
notes.explanation: Within one enterprise, the least restrictive setting usually wins, with some exceptions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “What about users with multiple licenses?”
notes.evidence: A user can receive access to Copilot from multiple organizations in the same enterprise. If these organizations have configured the same policy differently, the least restrictive policy usually applies

notes.front: A user has licences from two different enterprises, and one disables Copilot Chat in GitHub. What almost always happens?
notes.back: The feature is disabled: across enterprises, the most restrictive policy almost always applies.
notes.explanation: This is the reverse of the rule for organizations within one enterprise, and it is rarer.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “What about users with multiple licenses?”
notes.evidence: More rarely, if a user receives a license from multiple different enterprises, the most restrictive policy across enterprises almost always applies. For example, if any enterprise disables Copilot Chat in GitHub, that feature is disabled for the user.

notes.front: Licences from several organizations in one enterprise versus from several enterprises: which policy wins in each case?
notes.back: Several organizations: the least restrictive, usually. Several enterprises: the most restrictive, almost always.
notes.explanation: Keep the hedges: neither rule is absolute.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “What about users with multiple licenses?”
notes.evidence: the least restrictive policy usually applies, but there are some exceptions. More rarely, if a user receives a license from multiple different enterprises, the most restrictive policy across enterprises almost always applies.

notes.front: Can you name two surfaces where Copilot policies can apply?
notes.back: Any two of: editors, the GitHub website, or Copilot CLI.
notes.explanation: Policies reach any surface where users authenticate to Copilot, though not every policy applies to every surface.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “Where do policies apply?”
notes.evidence: Policies can apply to any surface where users authenticate to Copilot, including IDEs, the GitHub website, and Copilot CLI. However, not all policies apply to every surface.

notes.front: What two steps does GitHub suggest to prevent Copilot policy drift?
notes.back: Regularly review who has access to policy settings, and use the audit log to monitor policy changes.
notes.explanation: Drift is a risk when many people can change policies and governance is not clearly communicated.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, GitHub Copilot policies for enterprises and organizations, “How can I prevent policy drift?”
notes.evidence: Regularly review the people with access to policies:

notes.front: With Copilot Business or Enterprise and “Copilot in GitHub.com” enabled, which two extra options appear?
notes.back: Opt in to user feedback collection, and opt in to preview features.
notes.explanation: Preview features may have flaws and may be changed or discontinued at any time.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization, “Opting in to previews or feedback”
notes.evidence: If your organization has a Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise plan and you enable "Copilot in GitHub.com", two additional options are displayed:

notes.front: Which third-party coding agents can an organization allow, and which repositories can they reach?
notes.back: Anthropic Claude and OpenAI Codex; they reach the same repositories that Copilot cloud agent is enabled in.
notes.explanation: In an enterprise-owned organization, the settings appear only if an enterprise admin has enabled third-party agents.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization, “Enabling or disabling third-party coding agents in your repositories”
notes.evidence: You can choose whether to allow the following coding agents to be enabled in your organization: * Anthropic Claude * OpenAI Codex Coding agents have access to the same repositories that Copilot cloud agent has been enabled in.

notes.front: If you receive Copilot from an organization, what must the organization do before you can use Copilot code review on GitHub.com?
notes.back: Enable the “Copilot code review” option in its Copilot policy settings.
notes.explanation: The requirement covers reviews on GitHub.com and in GitHub Mobile.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, About GitHub Copilot code review, “Availability”
notes.evidence: If you receive Copilot from an organization, your organization must enable the **Copilot code review** option in the Copilot policy settings. This applies to reviews on GitHub.com or in GitHub Mobile.

notes.front: Members of an organization on Copilot Business see no Copilot option under Reviewers on their pull requests. What should the owner check first?
notes.back: D: that the “Copilot code review” policy is enabled.
notes.choices:
A) That a prompt file exists
B) That each member has Copilot Pro+
C) That the audit log is being streamed
D) That the “Copilot code review” policy is enabled
notes.choicesExplained: B: licensed members are governed by the organization’s policies, not personal plans. C: streaming keeps history and does not switch features on. A: prompt files are an editor feature.
notes.explanation: For users who get Copilot from an organization, code review on GitHub.com depends on that policy being on.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, About GitHub Copilot code review, “Availability”
notes.evidence: your organization must enable the **Copilot code review** option in the Copilot policy settings.

notes.front: Is the policy that allows members without a Copilot licence to use code review on or off by default?
notes.back: Off: it is disabled by default.
notes.explanation: Once set at enterprise level, the policy is visible but not editable at organization level.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, About GitHub Copilot code review, “Enabling code review for users without a license”
notes.evidence: The second policy has these characteristics: * It is disabled by default. * Once this policy is set at the enterprise level, it becomes **visible, but not editable** at the organization level.

notes.front: How does an organization owner turn on automatic Copilot code review across chosen repositories?
notes.back: With an organization branch ruleset whose branch rules include “Automatically request Copilot code review”.
notes.explanation: The ruleset targets repositories by name pattern, so one rule can cover many repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot, “Configuring automatic code review for repositories in an organization”
notes.evidence: Under "Branch rules," select **Automatically request Copilot code review**.

notes.front: In an automatic-review ruleset, why might you select “Review draft pull requests”?
notes.back: To catch errors early, before a human review is requested.
notes.explanation: Without it, Copilot does not review a pull request while it is still marked as a draft.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot, “Configuring automatic code review for repositories in an organization”
notes.evidence: Optionally, if you want Copilot to review pull requests while they are still drafts, select the **Review draft pull requests**. This can be a useful option for catching errors early, before requesting a human review.

notes.front: When does billing for a Copilot Business seat start?
notes.back: When you grant the member access, whether or not they ever use Copilot.
notes.explanation: Granting a seat, not first use, is the billing event.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Granting access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “Configuring access to GitHub Copilot in your organization”
notes.evidence: Billing for GitHub Copilot starts when you grant an organization member access, irrespective of when they first use Copilot.

notes.front: If you grant a member Copilot midway through a billing cycle, the cost is {{c1::prorated}} for the rest of the cycle.
notes.explanation: You pay only for the part of the cycle in which the seat exists.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Granting access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “Configuring access to GitHub Copilot in your organization”
notes.evidence: If you grant an organization member access midway through a billing cycle, the cost is prorated for the remainder of the cycle.

notes.front: On an organization’s Copilot Access page, which two choices decide who gets seats?
notes.back: “Purchase for all members” (all current and future users) or “Purchase for selected members” (chosen teams or users).
notes.explanation: Selected members can be added one by one through search, or in bulk by uploading a file.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Granting access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “Granting access to GitHub Copilot for all current and future users in your organization”
notes.evidence: To enable GitHub Copilot for all current and future users in your organization, select **Purchase for all members**.

notes.front: To save money, an owner grants Copilot seats to 50 developers now but says “we won’t pay until they start using it”. What is wrong?
notes.back: A: billing starts when access is granted.
notes.choices:
A) Billing starts when access is granted, whatever the use
B) Nothing: seats are free for the first cycle
C) Seats can only be granted to all members at once
D) Nothing: billing starts at first use
notes.choicesExplained: D: first use is not the trigger. B: no free first cycle is described; mid-cycle grants are prorated. C: seats can go to selected members.
notes.explanation: A granted seat is billed even if it is never used.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Granting access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “Configuring access to GitHub Copilot in your organization”
notes.evidence: Billing for GitHub Copilot starts when you grant an organization member access, irrespective of when they first use Copilot.

notes.front: If an organization removes a member’s Copilot seat during a billing cycle, when does the member lose access?
notes.back: At the start of the next billing cycle; they keep access for the rest of the current one.
notes.explanation: Organization-level removal takes effect from the next cycle, not at once.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Revoking access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “About organization-level revocation”
notes.evidence: For people whose access is revoked through organization-level revocation, the removal takes effect from the start of the next billing cycle. If you remove a seat during a cycle, the user will have access to Copilot for the remainder of the billing cycle.

notes.front: An organization revokes a user’s Copilot, but the user also has access through an enterprise team. What happens?
notes.back: They keep Copilot: organization revocation removes only access that came through that organization.
notes.explanation: An enterprise owner must remove them from the enterprise team or unassign the licence, which revokes access immediately.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Revoking access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “About organization-level revocation”
notes.evidence: Revoking access at the organization level only removes access for people who receive Copilot through the organization. If a person also has access through an enterprise team or as an individual, they will retain it.

notes.front: What happens to a member’s Copilot seat when they are removed from the organization that granted it?
notes.back: Their Copilot access is revoked automatically.
notes.explanation: You can also revoke Copilot alone and keep them as a member.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Revoking access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “Revoking access to Copilot for specific users in your organization”
notes.evidence: Removing a user from the organization(s) that had granted them Copilot access will automatically revoke their Copilot access. Alternatively, you can revoke Copilot access while preserving their organization membership.

notes.front: On the 10th of the month, an owner cancels Omar’s organization seat. On the 20th Omar is still using Copilot. Why?
notes.back: C: removal takes effect from the next billing cycle.
notes.choices:
A) The cancellation failed
B) Seats can only be cancelled through the REST API
C) Removal takes effect from the next billing cycle
D) He must first be removed from the organization
notes.choicesExplained: A: continued access is expected until the cycle ends. B: seats can be cancelled in settings too. D: removing him from the organization is one way to revoke, not a requirement.
notes.explanation: A seat removed mid-cycle keeps working for the rest of the cycle.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Revoking access to GitHub Copilot for members of your organization, “About organization-level revocation”
notes.evidence: If you remove a seat during a cycle, the user will have access to Copilot for the remainder of the billing cycle.

notes.front: Which audit log search term shows all events related to your Copilot plan?
notes.back: `action:copilot`.
notes.explanation: You can narrow it to one event, such as `action:copilot.cfb_seat_assignment_created` for a licence assigned to a new user.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Searching audit log events”
notes.evidence: Use the `action:copilot` search term to view all events related to your Copilot plan.

notes.front: Does the audit log include the prompts a user sends to Copilot locally?
notes.back: No. Client session data is not included; getting it needs a custom solution.
notes.explanation: Some companies, for example, use custom hooks to send Copilot CLI events to their own logging service.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot”
notes.evidence: The audit log does **not** include client session data, such as the prompts a user sends to Copilot locally. A custom solution is required to access this data

notes.front: To view a record of agent activity in the audit log, search for {{c1::`actor:Copilot`}}.
notes.explanation: Agent activity is filtered by who acted (the actor), not by the kind of action.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Searching audit log events”
notes.evidence: To view a record of agent activity, use the `actor:Copilot` search term.

notes.front: An auditor wants to see which pull requests Copilot’s agents created last month. Which audit log search term should she start with?
notes.back: C: `actor:Copilot`.
notes.choicesExplained: A shows events about the Copilot plan, such as settings and licences. B shows licences assigned to new users. D is not a documented search term.
notes.explanation: Agent activity is found by the actor, and agentic events record actions such as creating a pull request.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Searching audit log events”
notes.evidence: To view a record of agent activity, use the `actor:Copilot` search term.

notes.front: A security lead needs every change to Copilot settings, policies and licences in the enterprise. Which search term fits?
notes.back: D: `action:copilot`.
notes.choicesExplained: A shows agent activity, not plan changes. B is a field in agentic events, not the plan search. C is not a documented search term.
notes.explanation: Plan changes, such as settings, policies and licences, are Copilot events found with the action search.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Searching audit log events”
notes.evidence: Use the `action:copilot` search term to view all events related to your Copilot plan.

notes.front: The audit log retains events for the last {{c1::180}} days.
notes.explanation: For longer history, GitHub recommends streaming the log elsewhere.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Retaining audit log history”
notes.evidence: The audit log retains events for the last 180 days.

notes.front: A regulator asks for two years of Copilot policy changes. What does GitHub recommend so this is possible?
notes.back: D: stream the audit log to a security information and event management platform.
notes.choices:
A) Export Copilot Chat history
B) Search the audit log with `action:copilot`; it keeps all history
C) Ask GitHub Support to extend retention
D) Stream the audit log to a security information and event management platform
notes.choicesExplained: B: the log keeps only the last 180 days. C: no such extension is described. A: chat history is not where policy changes are recorded.
notes.explanation: Such a platform lets you view long-term history and set up alerts for anomalous activity.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Reviewing audit logs for GitHub Copilot, “Retaining audit log history”
notes.evidence: We recommend streaming the audit log to a Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platform, where you can view long-term history and set up alerts for anomalous activity.

notes.front: In an agentic audit log event, what does the `agent_session_id` field link to?
notes.back: The specific agent session that generated the event.
notes.explanation: It appears only when the event is the result of an agent session; `actor_is_agent` is always `true` in such events.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, Audit log events for agents, “Audit log events for agents”
notes.evidence: A unique identifier linking to the specific agent session that generated the event. This field only appears when the event is the result of an agent session.

notes.front: What is the release status of the REST API endpoints for Copilot user management?
notes.back: Public preview, subject to change.
notes.explanation: Scripts built on them may need updating as the endpoints change.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “REST API endpoints for Copilot user management”
notes.evidence: These endpoints are in public preview and subject to change.

notes.front: Which REST API endpoint gets an organization’s Copilot subscription information, including seat breakdown and feature policies?
notes.back: `GET /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing`.
notes.explanation: It only reads the settings; to change them you go to the organization’s settings on GitHub.com.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “Get Copilot seat information and settings for an organization”
notes.evidence: Gets information about an organization's Copilot subscription, including seat breakdown and feature policies. To configure these settings, go to your organization's settings on GitHub.com.

notes.front: Which REST API endpoint lists every Copilot seat an organization is currently being billed for?
notes.back: `GET /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/seats`.
notes.explanation: Each seat object includes the user’s most recent Copilot activity.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “List all Copilot seat assignments for an organization”
notes.evidence: Lists all Copilot seats for which an organization with a Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise subscription is currently being billed.

notes.front: A seat’s `last_activity_at` shows no editor use, though the user codes with Copilot daily. What is a likely reason?
notes.back: Telemetry is disabled in their editor; editor activity is only reflected when it is enabled.
notes.explanation: An empty activity date is not proof that a seat is unused.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “List all Copilot seat assignments for an organization”
notes.evidence: Users must have telemetry enabled in their IDE for Copilot in the IDE activity to be reflected in last_activity_at.

notes.front: Which REST API endpoint gives Copilot seats to named members of an organization?
notes.back: `POST /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/selected_users`.
notes.explanation: The organization needs a Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise subscription and a configured suggestion matching policy.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “Add users to the Copilot subscription for an organization”
notes.evidence: Only organization owners can purchase Copilot seats for their organization members. The organization must have a Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise subscription and a configured suggestion matching policy.

notes.front: Which REST API endpoint returns one organization member’s Copilot seat details?
notes.back: `GET /orgs/{org}/members/{username}/copilot`.
notes.explanation: It covers a member who currently has access, and includes their most recent Copilot activity.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “Get Copilot seat assignment details for a user”
notes.evidence: Gets the GitHub Copilot seat details for a member of an organization who currently has access to GitHub Copilot.

notes.front: What does `POST /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/selected_teams` do?
notes.back: It purchases a Copilot seat for every user in each specified team.
notes.explanation: The organization is billed for each seat at its Copilot plan’s rate.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “Add teams to the Copilot subscription for an organization”
notes.evidence: Purchases a GitHub Copilot seat for all users within each specified team. The organization will be billed for each seat based on the organization's Copilot plan.

notes.front: Calling `DELETE /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/selected_users` sets the named users’ seats to {{c1::“pending cancellation”}}.
notes.explanation: The response gives the total number of seats set to that state.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “Remove users from the Copilot subscription for an organization”
notes.evidence: Sets seats for all users specified to "pending cancellation".

notes.front: After `DELETE /orgs/{org}/copilot/billing/selected_teams`, when do the team’s members lose Copilot?
notes.back: At the end of the current billing cycle, unless they keep access through another team.
notes.explanation: Their seats go to “pending cancellation” rather than ending at once.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, REST API endpoints for Copilot user management, “Remove teams from the Copilot subscription for an organization”
notes.evidence: This will cause the members of the specified team(s) to lose access to GitHub Copilot at the end of the current billing cycle unless they retain access through another team.

notes.front: A script calls `DELETE …/selected_users` for Priya, who is also in a team that has Copilot seats. What happens to her access?
notes.back: D: she keeps access through her team membership.
notes.choices:
A) It ends immediately
B) It ends at the end of the billing cycle, whatever her teams
C) The call fails because she is in a team
D) She keeps access through her team membership
notes.choicesExplained: A: removal sets “pending cancellation”, not an immediate end. B ignores the team exception. C: nothing says the call fails.
notes.explanation: Pending cancellation ends access at the cycle’s end only for users who do not keep it through a team.
